{{Short description|Two continuous functions can be glued together to create another continuous function}}
In [[topology]], the '''pasting''' or '''gluing lemma''', and sometimes the '''gluing rule''', is an important result which says that two [[continuous function]]s can be "glued together" to create another continuous function. The [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]] is implicit in the use of [[piecewise function]]s. For example, in the book ''Topology and Groupoids'', where the condition given for the statement below is that <math>A \setminus B \subseteq \operatorname{Int} A</math> and <math>B \setminus A \subseteq \operatorname{Int} B.</math>

The pasting lemma is crucial to the construction of the [[fundamental group]] and [[fundamental groupoid]] of a [[topological space]]; it allows one to concatenate [[path (topology)|path]]s to create a new path.

==Formal statement==

Let <math>X,Y</math> be both [[closed set|closed]] (or both [[open set|open]]) subsets of a topological space <math>A</math> such that <math>A = X \cup Y</math>, and let <math>B</math> also be a topological space. If <math>f : A \to B</math> is continuous when [[restriction (mathematics)|restricted]] to both <math>X</math> and <math>Y,</math> then <math>f</math> is continuous.{{sfn|Dugundji|1966|p=83|loc=Theorem III.9.4}}

This result allows one to take two continuous functions defined on closed (or open) subsets of a topological space and create a new one.

'''Proof''': if <math>U</math> is a closed subset of <math>B,</math> then <math>f^{-1}(U )\cap X</math> and <math>f^{-1}(U) \cap Y</math> are both closed since each is the [[preimage]] of <math>f</math> when restricted to <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> respectively, which by assumption are continuous. Then their [[union (set theory)|union]], <math>f^{-1}(U)</math> is also closed, being a finite union of closed sets.

A similar argument applies when <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> are both open. <math>\Box</math>

The infinite analog of this result (where <math>A = X_1 \cup X_2 \cup X_3 \cup \cdots</math>) is not true for closed <math>X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots.</math> For instance, the [[inclusion map]] <math>\iota : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}</math> from the [[integer]]s to the [[real line]] (with the integers equipped with the [[cofinite topology]]) is continuous when restricted to an integer, but the preimage of a [[bounded set|bounded]] open set in the reals with this map is at most a finite number of points, so not open in <math>\mathbb{Z}.</math>

It is, however, true if the <math>X_1, X_2, X_3\ldots</math> form a [[locally finite collection]] since a union of locally finite closed sets is closed. Similarly, it is true if the <math>X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots</math> are instead assumed to be open since a union of open sets is open.
